rationale: A wins because it keeps the strongest story as a question, not a slogan: “top creators collectively” is treated as a self-selected numerator with an undisclosed denominator. B has usable bones, but “Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model” asserts a fact the update never gave it. A also finds a real human protagonist in “A writing platform is now asking writers to become video producers,” while B mostly circles platform strategy and unit economics.
gaps_in_A: “Substack has stopped competing with Mailchimp and started competing with YouTube” imports named competitors not supplied in the update, then awkwardly refuses “Substack takes on YouTube” as slop. Pick one standard and live by it.
“the people who chose Substack precisely because it was text now face a feed that rewards something they didn't sign up to make” assumes creator motivation and feed rewards before the proof is in.

“Video hosting is one of the most expensive infrastructure commitments a platform can make” may be true, but it is external scaffolding. The angle correctly asks for cost proof, but the body leans on the premise early.
gaps_in_B: “Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model” invents the ad-model fact. The update says Substack takes a 10% subscription cut; it does not say there are no ads or no other revenue lines.
“its revenue is capped at 10% of subscriptions” overclaims. A 10% take rate is supplied; a revenue cap is not.
“The prevailing belief is real and widely held: short-video feeds are ad businesses” is a contrarian foundation with no source in the update. That is not seasoning; that is the load-bearing wall.
B misses the creator-labor story. No angle makes the affected writer the protagonist, which is the most reportable human consequence of asking a text platform to become video-native.
